extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors / patent attorneys drafting and prosecuting AI/ML-related patent applications (primarily before the USPTO)
extracted.subtask_short: patent drafting and prosecution for AI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting specifications and claims, performing prior-art searching, and handling prosecution (especially 35 U.S.C. § 101 and § 103 rejections) for inventions involving artificial intelligence and machine learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish AI/ML terminology and concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear distinctions between AI in the general sense, ML, deep learning, NLP, and related terms so they are not conflated or used merely as marketing language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly describe AI/ML concepts (do not laboriously re-explain well-known concepts) but ensure terminology is precise so examiners cannot misconstrue the invention. Example: note that not all AI is NLP and not all NLP is AI (e.g., stop-word removal is NLP but may not be AI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify the invention: improving AI vs using AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the invention (1) improves AI/ML itself (models, training processes, hardware) or (2) uses AI/ML to improve another field, because each type requires different drafting and prosecution approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions improving AI often involve math/technical detail and are easier to prosecute and less likely to face §101 trouble; inventions using AI commonly land in non-AI art units, face more §101 and §103 scrutiny, and require different claim/context strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art searching tailored to AI invention type
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a comprehensive prior art search using internet sources and patent databases, with search sources differing by invention type (research papers/university publications/patent apps for AI-improvement inventions; broader internet and marketing materials for inventions using AI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on inventors for prior art; ask inventors targeted questions (e.g., differences from references; implementation difficulties; why chosen ML type is appropriate; special aspects of input/output data). Internet posts and ‘wouldn’t it be cool’ discussions can be significant prior art for AI-using inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid under-explaining AI (do not treat it as a black box)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not under-explain how AI/ML is implemented; treating AI as a black box invites §102/§103, §101, and §112 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification should explain how the ML model is trained (supervised/unsupervised; labeled/unlabeled), model type(s), training data characteristics, input data structure/examples, and expected output types (Boolean, selection, percentage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-explaining well-known AI concepts (be concise)
rubrics_metrics.description: While you must explain implementation-specific details, avoid lengthy re-explanations of basic AI/ML concepts that are unnecessary and likely ignored by examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a brief background but focus disclosure on what is novel about your implementation and the concrete technical details relevant to the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not describe AI as human-like thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid language suggesting the AI 'decides', 'weighs', or 'thinks' in human terms; such language invites §101 rejections by analogizing steps to mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace human-like phrasing with precise technical descriptions (e.g., 'outputs a Boolean value' and then 'based on that Boolean the system proceeds'). Review and edit specification and claims to remove anthropomorphic phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid black-box claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely state 'determining, via a machine learning model, whether to trigger an alarm' or similar black-box formulations are vulnerable to obviousness and eligibility rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide claim detail that shows how the ML is applied and linked to technology so examiners cannot treat the ML as a conventional algorithm substitution. Include intermediate steps and technical context rather than only high-level outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing impossible actions to ML (no 'AI magic')
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not recite actions the ML model itself cannot perform (e.g., 'triggering, by a machine learning model, an alarm') when in practice the model outputs data used by other components to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claims so that the ML outputs are received and then cause downstream system actions (e.g., ML outputs a Boolean → system triggers alarm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple AI-specific active claim steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should explicitly recite multiple active steps specific to ML to highlight technical distinctions from conventional algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpful steps include: (1) training an ML model (describe training method and data), (2) providing formatted input to the trained model (describe input format), (3) receiving particular output from the model (describe output type), (4) utilizing the output (cause a physical or technological change), and (5) retraining the model (feedback loop). Explicitly reciting these steps helps resist §102/§103 and §101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize retraining / feedback loops when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Including retraining of the ML model based on subsequent activity (e.g., user feedback) is viewed by examiners as a strong claim element and 'gold standard' for ML claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and specification to show how retraining occurs (what data used, how weights change, what triggers retraining) to argue the invention improves the algorithm over time and is more than a static mental process or conventional computing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear claim structure and, where appropriate, emulate USPTO Example 39
rubrics_metrics.description: Review and, where applicable, emulate the structure/approach of Example 39 of the USPTO's Subject Matter Eligibility Examples: Abstract Ideas to defend against §101 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 39's iterative training algorithm and multi-stage neural network training can be persuasive; similarity in structure can help persuade examiners but has limits (examiner may require similar multistep improvements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish multiple ML models in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention uses multiple task-specific ML models, explicitly distinguish them in claims (do not imply a single model performs disparate tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinal identifiers like 'first training data'/'second training data' or 'first output'/'second output' to avoid ambiguity and to make it harder to design around claims; multiple models can strengthen arguments against §101 and §103 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place AI steps in a technological context
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and specification should situate AI usage within preceding and following technological steps so the invention cannot be analogized to human mental processes or mere conventional hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe what generated the input data, how input is preprocessed for the AI, how output is subsequently used (e.g., trigger a physical change, modify speed), and overall system context. Contextualizing inputs/outputs helps resist §101 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: For inventions improving AI, claim specific technical aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention improves AI itself, focus claims on specific model aspects (nodes, weights), mathematical functions, training approaches, and how they improve performance (accuracy, speed, efficiency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend claims to explicitly indicate how particular steps improve the functioning of the ML model rather than claiming general decision-making improvements; this often overcomes §101 rejections for AI-improvement inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect increased examiner scrutiny and prepare to engage
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate that AI-related applications (especially those using AI) face heavier scrutiny, more §101 rejections, and potential placement in non-AI art units with examiners less familiar with AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for a prosecution 'battle'—use examiner interviews, thorough remarks, strategic amendments, and where helpful expert declarations. Build a persuasive 'story' about why the AI is technical and non-abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use persuasive prosecution strategies for §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Overcoming §101 rejections often relies on storytelling and contextual explanation rather than narrow legalistic quibbling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thematic examiner interviews (not formulaic step-throughs), prepare persuasive written remarks, avoid wasting time on weak arguments, consider filing 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 declarations from experts or inventors where appropriate, and emphasize technical improvements and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address §103 / prior-art rejections by focusing on differences in training, input/output, and context
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut obviousness arguments, emphasize how differently trained ML models, distinct input/output formats, and contextual use (including retraining) produce materially different results from prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show why two models are not equivalent if trained differently; explicitly refute examiner assertions that different inputs/outputs are analogous; emphasize retraining and downstream utilization as non-obvious technical features. Be prepared to substantially amend claims if needed and coordinate amendments with inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept 'do this, but with AI' as sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that boil down to performing a known task 'but with AI' are unlikely to survive art or eligibility rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the claim elements demonstrate technical innovation — e.g., novel training approaches, specific data formats, feedback loops, or concrete technological effects — rather than merely substituting ML for conventional algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical caution on AI as an inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not name AI as an inventor; current law (Thaler v. Vidal) and USPTO practice require inventors be natural persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage inventor assertions that an AI 'invented' the subject matter; treat AI as a tool used during ideation, analogous to software used by designers, and ensure human inventorship is properly asserted.
